data.title: Typhoon Dolphin: Hongkongers stuck in Okinawa prepare for low supplies, power cuts
data.description:
Hong Kong holidaymakers in Okinawa on Friday contended with depleted supermarket shelves, potential power cuts and violent weather as Typhoon Dolphin shut the Japanese island’s main airport and disrupted every direct flight home.
Social media images shared by Hong Kong-linked travel accounts showed empty bread shelves and torrential rain sweeping parts of the popular destination, although travellers said conditions varied significantly across the island.
Hong Kong travel account Papa Traveller said northern Okinawa, including the area around the Churaumi Aquarium, was experiencing “extremely heavy wind and rain”, while Naha in the south was temporarily caught in a gap between rainbands.

A Cantonese-language Okinawa page also posted a photograph of empty supermarket shelves and urged visitors, especially those staying in central and northern areas, to prepare candles and drinking water due to the possibility of electricity and water cuts.
But one traveller staying in Mihama observed calmer conditions, saying two major supermarkets still had sufficient supplies and there had been no panic buying.
Several major attractions and shopping centres, including DMM Kariyushi Aquarium and Aeon Mall Okinawa Rycom, were also closed on Friday because of the storm.
More than 500 flights were cancelled across southwestern Japan, and nearly 260,000 residents in Okinawa and Kagoshima prefectures were ordered to evacuate amid warnings of violent winds, heavy rain and high waves.

Naha International Airport closed on Friday, grounding all domestic and international flights, as Dolphin passed just north of Okinawa’s main island with maximum sustained winds of 144km/h (89.4mph).
All six Okinawa-bound flights scheduled to depart from Hong Kong on Friday were either cancelled or postponed, according to Hong Kong International Airport’s website.
HK Express cancelled flights 842, 844 and 824, while Hong Kong Airlines grounded 676 and 658.
Greater Bay Airlines flight 336D, originally scheduled to leave on Friday morning, was postponed until 5.15am on Monday.
All six flights scheduled to arrive in Hong Kong from Okinawa on Friday were also disrupted, with five cancelled and a Greater Bay Airlines service postponed until Monday.

Hong Kong’s Travel Industry Council said it estimated that there were only two to three tour groups in Okinawa, after communicating with major local tour agencies.
“All travellers are safe and are staying at their hotels for the time being,” executive director Fanny Yeung Shuk-fun said.
Steve Huen Kwok-chuen, executive director of EGL Tours, said his agency had two travel groups in Okinawa.
“The traffic has come to a standstill, and both tours have to stay in their hotels,” he said.
“All 35 travellers are safe and a tour group departing for Okinawa tomorrow has their flight delayed by a few hours, but all else is as per normal.”
Authorities in the prefecture said three men in their seventies suffered minor injuries, while about 240 people had sought shelter at evacuation centres across Okinawa by midday.

data.title: Tai Po inquiry sheds more light on final moments of firefighter Ho Wai-ho
data.description:
An independent inquiry into Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades has released further details about the final moments of fallen firefighter Ho Wai-ho, who died in the line of duty while responding to the blaze at Wang Fuk Court last November.
An interim report from an interdepartmental fire investigation task force was released by the government-appointed independent committee on Thursday. The disclosure included images of Ho’s gear recovered from the scene.

“The post-fire visual inspection revealed that [Ho] might have been in prolonged contact with hot or burning objects, resulting in severe fire damage to his [uniform],” the report read.
The document noted that his PBI Matrix tunic and trousers, which were designed to withstand extreme temperatures for brief periods, were heavily compromised.
It was also noted that his anti-flash hood, which should be non-flammable, and his helmet showed little to no signs of unusual damage.
“No unusual damage was observed on [Ho’s] anti-flash hood and helmet, apart from a crack in the visor, which might have been caused by contact with a sharp or hard object either prior to or during the fire”, the document read.

Ho’s rubber boots might have also been in prolonged contact with hot or burning objects, the report pointed out.
“It is believed that the intense heat or flames exceeded the boots’ protective capacity over an extended period,” the document said.
Ho was among 168 people killed in the fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po last November – Hong Kong’s deadliest blaze since 1948.

data.title: Beyond lithography: Chinese chip toolmaker achieves wafer polishing breakthrough
data.description:
Chinese chip-tool developers continue to make technical progress, with the latest breakthrough in wafer polishing – a critical manufacturing step that flattens and smooths silicon discs – even as the industry remains heavily dependent on foreign suppliers for more complex manufacturing procedures.
Hwatsing Technology, China’s leading producer of chemical mechanical polishing equipment, announced a new metrology system for six-inch wafers on Thursday. The ultra-precise measurement is designed to identify defects and ensure manufacturing consistency.
Wafers are thin, flat discs of semiconductor material that serve as the base for microchips, integrated circuits and electronic devices. Turning a raw wafer into a finished chip requires multiple steps, including coating the surface with photoresist, etching intricate layers and wiring microscopic transistors.
According to Hwatsing, its new measurement tool can be integrated directly into the polishing workflow – marking the country’s first six-inch metrology system paired with chemical mechanical polishing equipment. The set-up would enable real-time measurements before and after polishing, feeding live data back to the control system, the company said.
This direct integration could improve wafer uniformity and reduce waste, helping to address the inefficiencies of traditional production lines, it added.
Based in the northern city of Tianjin, Hwatsing reported that it had shipped the new system to an unnamed “leading domestic optical silicon materials producer”.
The system targets chips used in power devices, microelectromechanical systems and sensors, mostly with mature processing nodes. Such devices are widely used in electric vehicles, industrial equipment, consumer electronics and telecommunications infrastructure.
In terms of broader performance, domestic suppliers accounted for 21 per cent of China’s overall wafer-fabrication equipment market in 2025, while local wafer polishers enjoyed a higher rate of 39 per cent, according to a May report by brokerage Bernstein.
Hwatsing remained the “undisputed leader” in the domestic wafer polishing segment, supplying 85 per cent of the market, according to Bernstein. Across all competitors, Hwatsing’s share reached 37 per cent last year, up from 1 per cent in 2018, according to Chinese brokerage Soochow Securities.
However, the self-sufficiency rate for wafer metrology and inspection tools stood at just 10 per cent, despite domestic manufacturers recording a 63 per cent increase in revenue last year, it added.
Progress remains severely constrained in lithography – the strategic chipmaking technology dominated by Dutch giant ASML, which is barred from selling its most advanced deep-ultraviolet lithography systems and all-extreme-ultraviolet machines to China. According to Bernstein, there were “virtually no viable local alternatives” and “zero meaningful progress” in substituting the foreign technology.

data.title: Sugar for the pill: US$8b fund boosts Hong Kong’s biotech hub ambitions
data.description:
Hong Kong is stepping up its efforts to invest in a cluster of biotech companies, positioning itself as a linchpin in Beijing’s push to reach new levels of innovation and challenge the United States for dominance in the global pharmaceutical market.
Hong Kong Investment Corporation (HKIC), which manages about US$8 billion in assets and is wholly owned by the Hong Kong government, has built a biotech and healthcare technology investment portfolio covering both traditional Chinese and Western drugs to help transform the city into a global biotech hub.
“We have a pretty diversified portfolio covering upstream [to] downstream [of the full healthcare value chain], including Chinese medicine, Western medicine, [products] ranging from prevention, diagnostic treatments and [surgical] operations,” HKIC CEO Clara Chan Ka-chai said at the Global Health Summit in Hong Kong on Friday.
She added that HKIC has been linking AI and large language model firms with drug discovery companies in its portfolio, making the process of finding new medicines “cheaper, faster and better”.
HKIC has invested in more than 200 companies “covering high growth, high impact sectors, including biotech and health tech”, Chan said at the event, adding that the internal rate of return on the portfolio since its inception was 14 per cent as of end-2025.
The discussion among medical professionals and political leaders at the summit about Hong Kong’s role came as the rivalry between China and US in the pharmaceutical and life sciences sector has intensified. Washington has rolled out a series of measures including the Biosecure Act in December, targeting China’s biotech ambitions.
On Wednesday, China’s Ministry of Commerce placed US DNA-authentication firm Applied DNA Sciences on a “countermeasures list”, accusing it of assisting US sanctions against Chinese companies over allegations of forced labour in western China’s Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region.
China’s innovative drug development is closing the gap with the US, said Lu Shun, a medical professor at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, at the event.
China was the first country to complete research on a drug resistance problem that affects about 15 per cent of lung cancer patients with an EGFR gene mutation, Lu said. “The drug’s indication has currently only been approved in China and is about two years ahead of the US.”
“In the field of antibody-drug conjugates, we are basically at the same level as the United States,” he added.

Meanwhile, Ko Wing-man, director of New Frontier GBA Healthcare, said that Hong Kong acts as a bridge between mainland manufacturing scale and global capital markets.
The city can “combine leading basic research … with mainland [China’s] enormous manufacturing capability, engineering excellence, and rapidly expanding innovation capacity”, said Ko, also a member of the Standing Committee, National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.
Ko added that Hong Kong could serve as “the international gateway for China’s life science industry”.
HKIC healthcare investment focuses include liquid biopsies, female health, and longevity science, she said. HKIC has also invested in Hong Kong-grown embodied-AI and surgical-robotics companies.
The fund has attracted more than US$8 of long-term market and international capital for every US$1 invested, Chan said. About 70 per cent of its investment capital has been put in early and growth-stage companies.
As of Friday, 11 companies in HKIC’s portfolio have listed in Hong Kong, with 30 more either having submitted or in the process of submitting their applications for an initial public offering in the city this year.
A surge of technology-driven listings, including healthtech and pharmaceutical innovators, has spurred Hong Kong’s bourse to overhaul its listing framework, aiming to better accommodate high-growth enterprises seeking access to international capital. The exchange is in the process of advancing reforms that would permit confidential filings and lower the market capitalisation threshold for eligible issuers.

data.title: HKU virologist spared conviction for assaulting man and damaging his phone
data.description:
A University of Hong Kong (HKU) virologist has been spared a criminal conviction for assaulting a man and damaging his mobile phone at a railway station last year.
Eastern Court on Friday placed Vijaykrishna Dhanasekaran on a two-year bind-over order and instructed him to pay HK$800 (US$102) in damages, after he admitted attacking a stranger at Hong Kong MTR station on August 17, 2025.
The 48-year-old associate professor, who heads the university’s pathogen evolution lab, could be fined HK$2,000 if he failed to keep the peace during the bind-over period.
The court heard Dhanasekaran was involved in a “trivial dispute” with retiree Raimundo Kwok Chun-tung, 56, inside a lift connecting to the Airport Express shortly after 6pm.
Dhanasekaran used his mobile phone to film Kwok, who then used his phone to film the defendant in return.
In the heat of the moment, the defendant knocked Kwok’s Samsung Galaxy Note 20 to the ground, then pushed him several times and kicked the HK$3,000 phone out of the lift.
A civil servant who witnessed the incident called police. Dhanasekaran remained silent under caution.
Kwok sustained scratches to his left arm and cuts to his left knee, while reporting mild pain in his right hip. He spent HK$800 to repair the cracked screen and dents on his phone.
Prosecutors agreed to drop charges of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and criminal damage on the condition that the defendant accept the bind-over order.
Dhanasekaran joined HKU’s School of Public Health in 2020 while also holding research positions in Singapore and Australia, according to the university’s website. He was credited for his study on the worldwide resurgence of the deadly H5N1, the virus that causes bird flu.

data.title: Missing man, 58, found dead in Ma On Shan after days-long search effort
data.description:
Hong Kong police have found the body of a missing 58-year-old man in Ma On Shan, with his cause of death to be confirmed following an autopsy.
Officers received a report at around 12.50am on Friday from a passer-by who had spotted a man lying on the ground near a slope on Nui Po Shan in Ma On Shan.
Upon arrival at the scene, officers confirmed the death of the man, who was believed to be the missing person last seen at King Lam Estate in Tseung Kwan O on the afternoon of July 24.

The force received a report on the same day from the family of a man surnamed Chan, stating that they had lost contact with him.
A police spokeswoman said the man was suspected to have become lost.
Police, the Fire Services Department, the Government Flying Service and the Civil Aid Service had mounted a joint search and rescue operation for days before finding him.

data.title: China’s Kimi K3 AI model escapes a closed cyber test: researchers
data.description:
China’s top open-weight AI model Kimi K3 broke out of its isolated test environment during a cybersecurity evaluation, according to US security researchers, following similar high-profile incidents involving closed frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic that highlight the growing challenge of constraining AI behaviour.
Kimi K3, released last month by Beijing-based Moonshot AI, escaped from a supposedly isolated sandbox environment, accessed the open internet, and found solutions on the developer platform GitHub, US firm Frontier Security said in a blog post on Thursday.
The incident occurred when the firm tested Kimi K3’s defensive cybersecurity capabilities using a benchmark evaluation from the AI Security Institute – a UK government research organisation, according to Frontier Security researchers Paul Kassianik and Yaron Singer.
A “basic network misconfiguration” in the benchmark framework allowed Kimi K3 to flee its digital testing cage and look up answers on the internet, effectively cheating the test, they said.
Kimi K3’s escape, however, did not involve the hacking of an external system, unlike recent breaches caused by OpenAI and Anthropic models.

Last month, OpenAI said its flagship GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased, “even more capable” system broke out of a sandboxed environment and hacked the open-source developer platform Hugging Face to obtain secret information containing answers to an internal test.
Anthropic later disclosed that it had also identified three previous incidents where its Claude models – including Opus 4.7, Mythos 5 and an internal research model – breached the infrastructure of three undisclosed organisations.
Even without a direct hack, the Kimi K3 incident could still be “potentially more harmful” because of the model’s open-weight nature, which makes it publicly available to adversarial actors, Frontier Security said.
Kimi K3’s ability to circumvent its test parameters also reflected the model’s weaker internal safeguards, according to one of the researchers.
“It found the misconfiguration itself, by probing its own network settings,” Kassianik wrote on social media platform X on Friday. “Most publicly available frontier models have internal guardrails that stop them. K3 didn’t blink.”
Moonshot did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.
The rapidly advancing capabilities of frontier AI have heightened global cybersecurity concerns, pushing the role of widely accessible open-weight models to the centre of an escalating debate.
While critics warn that advanced open-weight models lower technical barriers for malicious actors, several US AI leaders have defended open-source systems’ key role in cyber defence.
American tech giants including Nvidia, Palantir and Meta Platforms last month signed an open letter urging Washington not to restrict open-weight models. While open models carried real risks, they also enabled cybersecurity defenders to detect and respond to emerging threats posed by AI-equipped attackers, the companies argued.
That point was underscored when Hugging Face had to rely on GLM-5.2, an open-weight model from Beijing-based Zhipu AI, to contain the OpenAI attack after major proprietary US models refused to process the security logs due to safety guardrails.

data.title: Hang Lung Properties names former Starbucks China head Leo Tsoi as new CEO
data.description:
Hong Kong developer Hang Lung Properties has tapped Leo Tsoi Tak Lun, CEO of Toys ‘R’ Us Asia and former head of Starbucks China, as its new CEO and executive director.
Tsoi will join Hang Lung Group and Hang Lung Properties on September 7 as CEO-designate and executive director ahead of formally assuming the CEO role on October 1. He succeeds Weber Lo Wai-pak, who retires on August 31 after serving as CEO for eight years, the developer said in a statement on Friday.
Tsoi’s appointment marks Hang Lung’s first CEO change since Adriel Chan took over from his father Ronnie Chan as chairman in 2024, in the latest leadership shift at the family-controlled property group.
Tsoi, 56, has more than three decades of experience in retail and business management in Asia. He currently serves as CEO of Toys ‘R’ Us Asia, where he expanded the brand’s appeal to the “kidult” segment, and revived business growth across Greater China and Southeast Asia, according to Hang Lung.

Prior to this role, he headed Starbucks China as CEO after holding several senior leadership positions in the US coffee giant. Earlier in his career, Tsoi “built a strong leadership foundation” at PepsiCo and Procter & Gamble Greater China, Hang Lung said.
“As I step into this role, I look forward to partnering with our talented team to strengthen relationships with stakeholders, tenants, and customers,” Tsoi said in a statement. “I am grateful to Adriel and the boards for their trust, and to Weber for laying down such a strong foundation to build upon.”
The developer announced the management shift in its half-year earnings released on July 31, noting that a CEO-designate had been appointed without naming them.
Chairman Adriel Chan said Tsoi’s track record of “driving growth through excellence” made him the best candidate to “lead Hang Lung into the next chapter”.
At a press conference announcing the group’s earnings, Chan credited Lo with leading the company through “challenging” years, which included the Covid-19 pandemic and China’s prolonged property downturn.
Hang Lung announced the retirement of Lo in December.
Additional reporting by Peggy Ye

data.title: Hong Kong preferred base as Chinese SOEs consolidate overseas accounts
data.description:
China’s central state-owned enterprises (SOEs) are consolidating scattered overseas accounts into unified treasury hubs, with Hong Kong emerging as their preferred base amid a broader crackdown on outflows of state cash.
Decades of overseas expansion had seen many SOEs build up assets in multiple jurisdictions, leaving cash management fragmented and making it harder for regulators and company headquarters to track liquidity, foreign-exchange risk and cross-border financing, analysts said.
Central SOEs now hold nearly 8 trillion yuan (US$1.1 trillion) in overseas assets across more than 180 countries and regions, spanning over 10,000 projects and entities, according to the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission (Sasac).
Since 2022, authorities in mainland China have pushed central SOEs to build treasury systems offering full visibility and tight control, a mandate later extended to their overseas units.
“Previously, overseas businesses were often managed independently by individual companies, leading to duplicated investment, fragmented assets and inefficient resource allocation,” said Zhou Lisha, a research director at Tsinghua University’s Institute for Modern State-owned Enterprises, in an interview with state financial newspaper Securities Times in April.
A coordinated approach helped central SOEs optimise assets, boost returns and better manage geopolitical and operational risks, Zhou added.
Hong Kong has emerged as a destination of choice, benefiting from its international banking system, deep capital markets, offshore yuan pool and close links with the mainland.


Telecoms operator China Unicom rolled out an upgraded overseas treasury platform in late 2024. By late 2025, the unit was managing more than 7 billion yuan in offshore funds across 30 currencies, while slashing payment processing times from 30 minutes to just 30 seconds.
State-owned China Railway Rolling Stock Corporation launched a dedicated treasury centre in Hong Kong in April 2024, achieving 95 per cent visibility over its global bank accounts.
State Power Investment, which established its Hong Kong treasury arm in 2017, managed assets of 50.88 billion yuan by late last year. State Energy and China Mobile have also set up treasury centres in Hong Kong.
The push coincides with tighter regulatory oversight. In January, Sasac introduced a “look-through” supervisory regime targeting overseas acquisitions and project financing. In April it established a new bureau dedicated to monitoring overseas state assets.
Look-through supervision seeks to identify underlying assets, risks and beneficiaries by examining layers of ownership, investment vehicles or contractual arrangements.
Hong Kong is seeking to capture more of this business by positioning itself as a global treasury management centre. In June, the city government unveiled an action plan aimed at attracting multinational corporate treasury centres, including measures on tax incentives, treaty expansion, talent development and industry promotion.
Christopher Hui Ching-yu, Hong Kong’s secretary for financial services and the treasury, told a forum in June that the city aimed to strengthen its role as a platform for companies “bringing in and going global”, encouraging firms to centralise fund management, asset allocation and risk control in Hong Kong.

data.title: Swire Pacific posts record first-half profit as investment surges to fresh high
data.description:
Swire Pacific – whose high-profile assets include Hong Kong’s flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways, Swire Properties and Swire Coca-Cola – logged a record first-half profit during the first six months of the year, with the company’s investment also hitting a new high.
The Hong Kong-based conglomerate posted a recurring underlying profit of HK$6.96 billion (US$887 million) for the first half of 2026, up 48 per cent year on year, it said in a filing with the Hong Kong exchange on Thursday.
“We are confident in the outlook for the remainder of the year,” said Guy Bradley, chairman of Swire Pacific, during a press conference in Hong Kong on Thursday. “There is plenty of money going out into investing for the future.”
The group’s level of investment has also hit a record high, with Cathay Group investing HK$150 billion, Swire Properties HK$100 billion, and Swire Coca-Cola 12 billion yuan (US$1.8 billion), the company said.
All of the investment will go into the group’s core markets of the Chinese mainland, Hong Kong and Southeast Asia, according to Bradley. “I don’t see any reason to stop investing in this part of the world,” he said.
Cathay Group – which operates several airlines including Cathay Pacific – performed solidly in the first quarter. While demand remained high in the second quarter, jet fuel prices rose sharply due to the conflict in the Middle East. Its first-half profit reached HK$2.83 billion, up 72 per cent year on year, according to the filing.
The airline group has committed about HK$150 billion for investments into its fleet, cabin and lounge products, and digital innovation.
Meanwhile, Swire Properties has allocated HK$100 billion for investment over the 10-year period from 2022 to 2032, with HK$50 billion earmarked for the mainland, according to the company. Nearly 70 per cent of that investment has already been committed, the group said in its filing.

The developer posted an underlying profit of HK$4.08 billion for the first half, up 11.5 per cent year on year. The improved result was primarily driven by residential trading profits, most notably from the completed sales of 6 Deep Water Bay Road in Hong Kong.
The company is focused on upgrading two flagship Hong Kong developments, Pacific Place and Taikoo Place, the filing said. Swire Properties also delivered a solid performance in the Chinese mainland, where it has seven projects under development.
Separately, Swire Coca-Cola logged significantly improved results in mainland China during the year to June, driven by stronger consumer sentiment and ongoing investment in e-commerce channels. It reported a first-half profit of HK$846 million, up 5 per cent year on year.
The company said it was pressing ahead with plans to invest 12 billion yuan in new facilities and equipment on the mainland. It recently opened two new facilities in Kunshan, Jiangsu province, and Guangzhou, Guangdong province, respectively.
Southeast Asia also remains an important growth market for Swire Coca-Cola, and its integration of new franchises in the region is progressing well, following sizeable recent investments, it said.
“Looking ahead, we do see an ongoing recovery in consumer sentiment and expect the operating environment to improve further in the rest of the year,” Bradley said. “We remain confident that our strategy of making long-term investments in our core markets is the right one.”
The company declared a first interim dividend of HK$1.50 per A share and HK$0.30 per B share, which represents an increase of 15 per cent compared with the first interim dividend in 2025.

data.title: How recharged SAIC and GM tie-up plans to catch up with top EV makers in China
data.description:
China’s SAIC Motor has extended its cooperation with General Motors by 20 years, renewing the joint venture through 2047 amid aggressive competition from home-grown rivals.
SAIC and GM, the largest carmakers in China and the United States, respectively, in terms of sales volume, signed the agreement on Wednesday, building on a partnership that began in 1995 and led to the SAIC-GM joint venture in 1997.
Wang Xiaoqiu, chairman of state-owned SAIC, said both sides should leverage their strengths in technology, branding, global distribution and local resources, opening new avenues for development with a global perspective.
The venture would launch at least 30 electric vehicle (EV) models in China by 2030, with the goal of “joining the major players” in the world’s largest EV market, GM said in a statement.
The renewal comes as sales from SAIC-GM and affiliates slumped from a peak of more than 4 million vehicles in 2017 to about 2.17 million units last year, according to data from SAIC. GM’s global car sales also shrank sharply to about 6.2 million units last year from over 10 million units in 2016.
Even if Chinese cars cannot enter the American market, the Chinese market is large enough that Chinese and US carmakers can continue to cooperate amicably
David Zhang, International Intelligent Vehicle Engineering Association
As of June, domestic brands like BYD and Leapmotor commanded nearly 70 per cent of the home market, thanks to their dominance in EV technologies, according to the China Passenger Car Association.
The extension was seen as necessary, as GM had a global production network and a loyal customer base, while SAIC had access to China’s powerful supply chain, according to David Zhang, general secretary of the Shanghai-based International Intelligent Vehicle Engineering Association.
“The car market is a cutthroat competition, with everyone vying to knock out the other players and be the last one standing,” said Zhang. “If the agreement were to be terminated rashly, both SAIC and GM would suffer significant losses.”
Zhang highlighted GM’s plants and sales channels across the world, which could help ship SAIC-made cars to overseas markets, especially North America, offering a unique edge to the Chinese carmaker amid escalating trade tensions.
Despite shrinking sales, GM-related affiliates still accounted for nearly 45 per cent – or about 1 million units – of SAIC’s new car sales in the first seven months of the year, according to SAIC sales data.
SAIC remained China’s largest carmaker by sales, delivering 2.38 million vehicles between January and July – spanning both petrol and electric models – narrowly ahead of BYD’s 2.2 million units, which were entirely EVs over the same period, according to sales data from SAIC and BYD.
SAIC has also benefited from its ownership of MG, a historic British brand merged into the group in 2007, which has led China-made car sales in Europe for 11 years in a row. Sales exceeded 300,000 units last year, SAIC data showed.
Yet MG was surpassed by BYD in western Europe in the past quarter, according to data from Germany-based consultancy Schmidt Automotive Research, underscoring the aggressive expansion of Chinese EV makers amid weakening demand and squeezed profits at home.
International marques also continued to push into the Chinese market, with Germany’s Volkswagen adopting advanced driving assistance systems developed by Xpeng and France’s Renault setting up a research and development centre in Shanghai.
The partnerships come even as trade barriers escalate, with the latest potential restriction from the US targeting carmakers with more than 15 per cent Chinese ownership.
The only way international carmakers could compete with Chinese carmakers was through collaboration with Chinese suppliers, said Tim Hsiao, head of the Greater China auto and shared mobility research team at Morgan Stanley, in an interview in April.
“Even if Chinese cars cannot enter the American market, the Chinese market is large enough that Chinese and US carmakers can continue to cooperate amicably,” said Zhang.

data.title: Endanger Hong Kong’s national security, and I’ll take you down, Chris Tang warns
data.description:
Hong Kong’s security chief has warned he will take down anyone who endangers national security, while also slamming an embattled press group for lacking credibility ahead of an already delayed leadership election.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said on Friday that the Hong Kong Journalists Association (HKJA) was “not a statutory organisation” and that candidates for its executive committee reportedly included no representatives from mainstream local media outlets, undermining its legitimacy.
“All the candidates this time are reportedly from foreign media, so-called free media, or online media. There is not a single person from Hong Kong’s mainstream media,” he said. “How can it call itself the Hong Kong Journalists Association?”
He also accused the group of running a “black box” election, saying it had neither published the names of candidates nor disclosed the final list of those elected.
Tang said the association developed a “tainted record” during the 2019 anti-government protests, accusing it of having “shielded rioters”, adopting a biased stance and counting among its ranks members who repeatedly broke the law.

He also accused the group of misleading the public over the national security trial of former media boss Jimmy Lai Chee-ying by claiming it was a press freedom issue, when judges had ruled Lai was guilty of colluding with foreign forces and that the case had “nothing to do with press freedom”.
“Regardless of what name or title you use, if you want to engage in acts that endanger national security, collude with external forces, or subvert state power, I will definitely nail you. Face the consequences,” he said.
Tang further cautioned against organisations abusing trade union names to pursue agendas unrelated to labour rights, saying authorities would investigate and prosecute them in accordance with the law.
The HKJA originally planned to elect a new executive committee in mid-June but extended the incumbent committee’s term by three months after failing to attract enough candidates during the nomination period.
The association has since secured the minimum five candidates required and plans to hold the election on August 8.
The South China Morning Post has contacted the HKJA for comment.

data.title: Nominations for Hong Kong’s Election Committee to run from October 7 to 20
data.description:
Nominations for Hong Kong’s powerful Election Committee will take place in October, with the vote for 982 seats of the 1,500-member body – which picks the city’s chief executive and some of the legislative candidates – taking place a month later.
A government spokesman said Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu had specified November 22 as the polling date for the committee’s subsector ordinary elections and that the relevant notice had been gazetted on Friday.
The spokesman added that the nomination period would run from October 7 to 20, and that the chief electoral officer would publish “in due course” a notice specifying the period within which nomination forms were to be submitted.
“The government will continue to work closely with the Electoral Affairs Commission to actively carry out preparatory work, with a view to ensuring that the elections will be conducted smoothly in an open, honest, fair, safe and orderly manner, with arrangements that are efficient and user-friendly,” he said.
The date of the election was earlier announced by the Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Bureau in a paper submitted to the Legislative Council in July.
Hong Kong’s Election Committee is composed of 1,500 members from five sectors comprising 40 subsectors. The coming vote will elect 982 members to the committee for a five-year term running from February 2027 to January 2032.
Its powers include nominating and electing the city’s chief executive, for which elections are set to take place in March next year. Lee’s five-year term will end by the end of next June.
Following Beijing’s electoral overhaul to ensure only “patriots” rule Hong Kong, the body was expanded and amassed new powers to select Legislative Council members.
Under the overhaul, prospective lawmakers need to secure a minimum of 10 votes – at least two from each of the committee’s five sectors – before they can stand for election.
The Election Committee also sends 40 representatives of its own choosing, some or all of whom can be from within its own ranks, to the enlarged 90-seat Legislative Council.

data.title: Hong Kong weighs dedicated offence to tackle persistent child sex abuse
data.description:
Hong Kong is “actively considering” creating a dedicated offence to target persistent sexual abuse of children, after more than 90 per cent of suggestions from a month-long public consultation backed a proposed overhaul of laws tackling sex crimes.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said on Friday that more than 6,000 suggestions were received throughout the consultation period, which began on July 7 and wrapped up on Wednesday.
“All in all, over 90 per cent of suggestions supported the amendment and raised constructive opinions,” he said.
Tang added that authorities would actively study calls to introduce a stand-alone offence covering persistent child sexual abuse, noting that the Hong Kong Bar Association had broadly endorsed the proposal after weighing various factors.
“The government will actively consider the relevant suggestion and maintain close communication with stakeholders, including members of the legal sector,” he said.
The month-long consultation sought views on proposals to modernise local sex offences laws, which are largely based on English legislation enacted in 1956.
The reform package includes proposals to redefine consent, strengthen protections for victims and update offences involving children and mentally incapacitated persons.

The government earlier said it planned to introduce the amendment bill to the Legislative Council within the year and complete the process within the current administration’s term.
Tang also addressed concerns over the proposed retention of the “mistaken belief in consent” defence, saying the bill already set out 11 circumstances in which a victim would be deemed not to have consented if the relevant facts were established by evidence.
While some submissions called for further tightening of the law, Tang said the government believed the proposed provisions could address many of the scenarios raised, but would continue studying the issue alongside other views received during the consultation before finalising the bill.
On the subject of AI-generated sexually explicit “deepfake” images, Tang said the issue would not be dealt with solely through the proposed sex offences reforms.
He noted that existing laws, including offences related to access to a computer with criminal or dishonest intent, as well as provisions on obscene publications, could already apply in some cases, while the Department of Justice was separately reviewing whether additional AI-related criminal offences were needed.

data.title: Hong Kong woman loses HK$69m to scammers posing as mainland Chinese officials
data.description:
A Hong Kong woman has been conned out of nearly HK$69 million (US$8.8 million) in a month-long scam involving fraudsters posing as mainland Chinese officials.
Police said on Friday that the 43-year-old woman received calls from people claiming to be mainland law enforcement officers, who accused her of committing a crime and demanded money to prove her innocence.
The victim transferred about HK$68.9 million to designated bank accounts in multiple transactions between July 2 and August 1.
She contacted police on Wednesday after becoming suspicious.
The Western district crime squad is investigating the case. No arrests have been made so far.
Fake-official phone scams remain among the most common forms of financial deception in Hong Kong.
Authorities revealed last month that more than 40 mainland students in the city had fallen victim to scammers impersonating Chinese law enforcement officers in the first quarter of this year. The largest case involved more than HK$8 million.

data.title: Backed by DeepSeek, Unitree seeks US$9b valuation in landmark robotics IPO
data.description:
The long-awaited initial public offering of Unitree Robotics, which values the Hangzhou-based firm at 60.99 billion yuan (US$9 billion), is set to serve as a valuation benchmark for China’s booming embodied-AI sector, buoyed by retail investor excitement and high-profile AI backers like DeepSeek.
Widely billed as “mainland China’s first humanoid stock”, Unitree has priced its IPO on Shanghai’s Star Market at 150.8 yuan per share, according to a filing released Thursday evening. The firm will sell 40.45 million new shares to raise 6.1 billion yuan – above its initial 4.2 billion yuan target.
Backers including AI unicorn DeepSeek and tech giant Tencent Holdings joined the strategic placement, alongside state-backed giants China National Petroleum Corp, China Southern Power Grid, China Telecom, Citic Securities and the National Council for Social Security Fund.
DeepSeek, which invested 141 million yuan bound by a three-year lock-up period, agreed to co-develop AI models and embodied-intelligence technology with Unitree. The two firms would also give each other priority access in areas such as robot procurement and AI model services, Unitree said.
A valuation ‘ceiling’
Unitree’s IPO would serve as a valuation anchor – and effectively the ceiling – for other companies in the embodied-intelligence space, said Zheng Hualiang, founder of Leap VC, a Hangzhou-based venture capital firm investing in AI hardware and foundational models.
Zheng’s team first backed Unitree in 2022 when its pre-money valuation was about 1 billion yuan. At the time, “its ability to traverse different terrain and motion control was clearly superior to companies building wheeled robots”, he said.
The listing comes as a wave of Chinese robotics start-ups – including Deep Robotics, Leju Robotics, AgiBot, X Square Robot and LimX Dynamics – race to enter public markets. Venture capital firms have already pushed valuations for top-tier start-ups beyond 20 billion yuan, sparking growing debate over a potential bubble in physical AI.

At 150.8 yuan per share, Unitree’s IPO implies a price-to-earnings ratio of 219.23 times and a price-to-sales (P/S) multiple of 35.89 times. For comparison, Hong Kong-listed peers UBTech Robotics and Dobot trade at P/S multiples of 19.37 times and 20.12 times, respectively, while remaining unprofitable.
Unlike most of its Chinese rivals, Unitree is profitable. The company recorded 1.7 billion yuan in revenue and 591 million yuan in adjusted net profit last year, according to its prospectus.
Retail enthusiasm
Despite high valuations, investor interest remains robust.
“If Unitree doesn’t get this listing right, it could make [fundraising] harder for the companies behind it,” said an employee at a rival Chinese robotics start-up who asked to be identified only by his surname Zhang. He said he planned to subscribe to the Unitree IPO on Monday despite having low expectations for getting an allotment.
Kathy Shi, a Shanghai-based retail investor, said she applied for shares as a bet on the listing premium rather than on near-term industry fundamentals. Shi said she did not expect large-scale commercial adoption of embodied intelligence any time soon, citing policy backing and Star Market excitement as her main drivers.
Unitree’s debut comes amid a volatile backdrop for mainland tech stocks.
Fears of overcrowded trades triggered sharp sell-offs in AI computing, semiconductors and optical modules last month. Shanghai’s tech-focused Star 50 Index swung wildly in July, closing the month down nearly 26 per cent.
Zheng cautioned that any broader rally across the robotics supply chain could prove short-lived unless shipment volumes scale rapidly.
“The secondary market may trade on the theme in the short term,” Zheng said. “Over the longer run, it still comes down to whether that [enthusiasm] translates into actual business.”
For now, Unitree retained a distinct edge over its competitors through low-cost mass production capabilities and strong consumer brand recognition, he added.

data.title: Hong Kong’s Lingnan University student union ceases operations after 6 decades
data.description:
The student union of Hong Kong’s Lingnan University has announced it will dissolve after nearly six decades in operation due to “changes in the situation both on and off campus”, marking the latest in a spate of closures among such organisations in recent years.
In a social media post on Thursday, the student union said it had passed a resolution to dissolve after holding a recent joint meeting. Its decision means that only two of Hong Kong’s public universities still have active student unions, one of which is no longer allowed to operate on campus.
“Since its establishment in 1967, the union has always upheld the spirit of unity and mutual help among students and actively maintained close ties with the university to seek the well-being of all Lingnan students,” it said.
“Furthermore, the union has been committed to addressing social issues for many years, promoting members’ social awareness and sense of responsibility in various ways, and contributing to the progress of Hong Kong society.”
The union explained that it had made the “difficult decision” to dissolve “due to changes in the situation both on and off campus in recent years, and after balancing various factors”. It did not specify what the changes were.
The organisation had faced a tumultuous period leading up to its dissolution.
Last year, two former and two current committee members were arrested for allegedly stealing nearly HK$1 million (US$127,450) to pay off credit card bills and personal loans, as well as to fund investment accounts.
Following the arrests, the university issued a statement saying it had no affiliation with the student union and accused its members and associate bodies of acts and statements “inconsistent with the core values” of the institution.
Hong Kong’s student unions were once a locus of political activism in the city, but many disbanded or ceased operations amid heightened institutional and legal scrutiny following the enactment of the city’s national security laws.
The latest announcement leaves only the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology with an active student union on campus among the city’s eight publicly funded institutions.
The City University of Hong Kong’s student union also remains active, but has been operating out of a space in Cheung Sha Wan after the university cut ties with it and ordered it to vacate campus premises in 2022.
Earlier this year, the University of Hong Kong’s student publication Undergrad ceased operations. The university had already severed ties with the student union in 2021, after it issued a statement that led to four of its leaders being jailed for advocating terrorism.
Last year, Baptist University suspended the operation of its student union after removing messages from campus that demanded justice for victims of the Tai Po fire. The suspension came on the heels of several arrests by police for alleged sedition in connection with the blaze.
The suspension was attributed to several reasons, including the low proportion of students holding union membership, the committee’s alleged lack of commitment to welfare and its perceived reluctance to comply with university regulations – all of which the union disputed.

The Chinese University of Hong Kong’s student union was one of the earliest to formally disband in 2021, after university management cut ties with the body, citing possible national security breaches.
Two of the university’s nine smaller college student unions continue to function, but the others have also disbanded.
Polytechnic University also terminated its relationship with its student union in April 2022, and took back the body’s office and facilities, effectively ending the union’s operations. The union has not elected a new executive committee since then.
The Education University of Hong Kong also stopped recognising its student union in 2022.

data.title: Hong Kong tourism sector urges action with visitor spending 44% below 2018 level
data.description:
Hong Kong’s tourism industry has called for more experiential events and closer cross-border cooperation to draw visitors, after tourist spending fell to HK$197.5 billion last year, 44 per cent below its 2018 level.
Lawmaker Perry Yiu Pak-leung, chairman of China Travel Service (Hong Kong) Limited, said on Friday that the fall reflected changing travel patterns, with tourists placing greater value on experiences and in-depth exploration than on shopping.
Yiu made the call after the latest Legislative Council research found that visitor spending had fallen 44 per cent, from about HK$353 billion in the pre-pandemic year of 2018.
Noting that lower visitor spending was a global trend, Yiu said some tourists still had strong purchasing power, but their spending depended on whether Hong Kong could encourage them to stay longer and offer a wider variety of events.
“The tourism industry is very much affected by the external environment, such as weather, flight prices and transport costs, among others,” he said.
“While we cannot control these factors, providing more and different travel experiences, and strengthening connections and synergy are some important directions to bring an upgrade to our industry, enhance tourists’ travel experience and boost their spending.”
According to the research, the gap between visitors’ spending in Hong Kong and Hongkongers’ expenditure abroad narrowed significantly in recent years.
While visitor spending in the city fell, Hong Kong residents’ non-local expenditure rose 10 per cent from 2018 to HK$191.1 billion last year.
The research also showed that spending per overnight visitor in Hong Kong fell from HK$6,614 in 2018 to HK$5,503 last year. Spending per same-day visitor dropped by more than 48 per cent over the same period, from HK$2,202 to HK$1,139.

It also cited Tourism Board figures showing that the share of overnight visitors’ spending on shopping fell from 51 per cent in 2018 to 36 per cent last year. Their spending on dining and activities, excluding hotel bills, rose from 28 per cent to 37 per cent.
The city recorded 49.9 million inbound visitor arrivals last year, about three-quarters of the 2018 peak of 65.1 million.
Meanwhile, Hongkongers made 117.5 million outbound trips last year, up 28 per cent from 2018. Northbound travel through cross-border land checkpoints accounted for 88 per cent of all departures.
Speaking on Friday, Yiu said the city had received more same-day visitors, who tended to spend less, as they transferred flights in Hong Kong or passed through cross-border checkpoints to mainland China.
While the city had hosted exhibitions to attract high-spending overnight business travellers, Hong Kong could also organise and promote more experiential events to appeal to visitors from different countries, he said.
He cited the example of working with the city’s Thai community and retailers to celebrate the Songkran festival, with the aim of attracting tourists from Southeast Asia.
Yiu also said industry practitioners had observed that more foreign travellers were reaching Hong Kong via the mainland, thanks to China’s 240-hour visa-free transit scheme.
The policy allows individuals from 55 eligible countries who are travelling from China to a third country or region to enter visa-free through designated ports and stay within permitted areas for up to 240 hours.
“Many travellers first travelled to the mainland and tried taking the high-speed rail to Hong Kong … If we step up cooperation with mainland cities, we can benefit from mutual tourist sourcing,” he said.
“We can lure foreign travellers and achieve multi-stop travel. I believe it will help increase visitor arrivals.”
He added that Greater Bay Area cities could also work together on promotion and tourism products to appeal to international travellers.

data.title: Temperatures could hit 36 degrees Celsius in Hong Kong over extremely hot weekend
data.description:
Temperatures in some parts of Hong Kong could hit 36 degrees Celsius (97 Fahrenheit) or above over the coming weekend under the influence of Tropical Cyclone Dolphin, according to the city’s forecaster, which warned residents to take precautions against heatstroke.
The Hong Kong Observatory said weak winds would linger over the city on Friday, with hot weather persisting over the next few days and pushing temperatures to 36 degrees or higher in certain parts of the New Territories.
“Under the influence of the outer subsiding air of Tropical Cyclone Dolphin, the weather will be extremely hot over the weekend,” the forecaster said.
Dolphin is expected to travel across the Ryukyu Islands and the East China Sea before moving towards the vicinity of Zhejiang and the northern part of Fujian.
“Members of the public should pay due attention to physical conditions and beware of heatstroke, especially when engaging in outdoor activities,” the Observatory said.
The intense heat on Friday coincides with a date on the Chinese lunar calendar that traditionally signifies the official commencement of autumn.
According to the Observatory’s latest nine-day forecast, the maximum temperature in Hong Kong on Friday will hit 34 degrees Celsius.
Isolated showers are expected in Hong Kong next Tuesday, with a southwesterly airstream forecast to affect the Guangdong coast by midweek.

data.title: In Focus|Hong Kong aims to be a global tech hub, but can it hold on to its young talent?
data.description:
At just 18, Hong Kong tech enthusiasts Rexan Wong Chak-chi and Ken Mochizuki are both rushing to deliver their business ideas.
However, their choices of launch pad could not be further apart. While Wong is eyeing Silicon Valley in the United States for better support, Mochizuki is keen to stay in the city and contribute to the local community.
Their contrasting approaches highlight Hong Kong’s advantages and challenges as it strives to become a global innovation and talent hub under China’s strategic blueprint, with artificial intelligence (AI) and research transformation listed among the priorities of the city’s first five-year plan, to be released by the government later this year.
While the city boasts cutting-edge university research, critics have warned that an increasingly risk-averse culture and a lack of early-stage support may push young tech talent towards overseas ecosystems.
California dreaming
Wong developed an interest in AI when he was 15 after joining a class on building mobile applications.
He later connected with many leading tech entrepreneurs through X, formerly known as Twitter, and built an AI-powered app called Text Behind Image in 2024. He said the app allowed its 500,000 users to design images with text behind featured objects.
Despite launching his first product in Hong Kong, Wong is looking to San Francisco and nearby Silicon Valley as the future launch pad for his AI business, believing the US tech hub can offer him better support.
“The main reason was really the access to support for early-stage founders. In Hong Kong, I think there is really a lack of support,” said Wong, a computer science undergraduate at the University of California, Santa Cruz.
“In San Francisco, there are a lot of incubators that help young founders go from zero to one.”
In January, he joined a two-month incubation programme with Founders Inc, a major San Francisco-based start-up community, making connections and receiving guidance from those with experience.
The “beauty” of the programme was having founders at different stages under the same roof, allowing them to discuss problems they faced, he said.
Intending to run an AI-powered market analytics company in the future, Wong is busy reaching out to tech start-ups in San Francisco and observing their operations.

Wong also pointed to the United States’ early adoption of advanced AI tools, such as models developed by Anthropic and OpenAI, as an advantage, while most Hongkongers used AI “at a very basic level” and some tools were not even available in the city.
“So it is really a lack of talent density, a lack of support and a lack of accessibility to these tools and knowledge on how to use frontier technology that holds Hong Kong back, which is why I picked San Francisco over Hong Kong,” he said.
Silicon Valley has been ranked the top start-up ecosystem in the world, while Hong Kong has come 29th, according to this year’s Global Startup Ecosystem Report, released by consultancy firm Startup Genome.
On a scale of one to 10, Hong Kong scored only two to four for its start-up performance, funding, talent, market reach and the degree to which it encourages AI start-ups. In contrast, Silicon Valley received full marks for each of these indicators.
Hong Kong only scored one for its research and development capacity, compared with Silicon Valley’s score of five.
Other Asian markets, such as Singapore and Seoul, and some major mainland Chinese cities, including Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen and Hangzhou, also outperformed Hong Kong.
Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation, said Beijing’s strength lay in its strong research capabilities, supported by top universities and close collaboration among the industrial, education and research sectors.
South Korea excelled because major enterprises devoted resources to research in key sectors such as semiconductors and biotechnology, while Singapore had outperformed Hong Kong because of its high density of venture capital firms and incubators – all of which Hong Kong could learn from, Shui added.
“If we cannot have our own major [tech] companies now, we should think about how to attract some of the largest institutions from other places to operate in Hong Kong,” he said.
According to the government’s investment arm, InvestHK, Hong Kong was home to 5,221 start-ups as of 2025, with 186 of them focusing on core or applied AI.
The San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley, has nearly 200,000 funded start-ups, with 80 per cent of funding going into AI, according to start-up data tracking platform dealroom.co.

‘A-Eye’ funding
But as Mochizuki sees it, Hong Kong’s young tech entrepreneurs are blessed with abundant support, and the only problem is that they are not told about available resources, so more publicity was needed.
Mochizuki, who is studying electrical engineering at City University (CityU), learned coding on his own in 2022, when he was still in secondary school and the Covid-19 pandemic forced pupils to study at home.
Within two years, he built “A-Eye”, an AI shopping assistant designed to help visually impaired people identify products and compare prices.
The project recently received HK$200,000 (US$25,500) in funding from CityU and the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP) through the university’s HK Tech 300 project.
CityU’s law school also offered free legal consultation under the programme, he added.
“My goal is to stay in Hong Kong and try to use my skills to contribute to this place and serve people,” Mochizuki said.
“Although other countries like the US or the United Kingdom may have better resources or a better culture for start-ups, the competition is much [fiercer] than in Hong Kong.”
Apart from university-based projects, Hong Kong authorities have made multiple start-up programmes available through the government-backed HKSTP and Cyberport.
HKSTP offers a range of start-up support programmes covering different stages, including ideation, incubation, acceleration and global expansion.
According to its latest annual report, 570 start-ups graduated from its support programme in 2024-25, and it spent more than HK$415 million on incubation and tenant support during the period.
Cyberport had more than 200 start-ups graduate from its entrepreneurship schemes in 2025-26, including an incubation programme offering grants of up to HK$500,000 and rental subsidies of up to HK$200,000, as well as the Creative Micro Fund, which helps early-stage start-ups move towards incubation.
The Home and Youth Affairs Bureau has also launched a funding scheme for young entrepreneurs to start their businesses in Hong Kong, Macau and the nine Guangdong cities under Beijing’s Greater Bay Area blueprint.
Shui said funding for early-stage start-ups remained insufficient as local investors preferred “easier and more certain” options, and investment activity tended to be cautious amid a turbulent economic environment.
“Tech start-ups have a higher chance of failure, but when they succeed, they can bring high returns,” he said, urging the government to step up support for early-stage founders.
A start-up usually goes through multiple rounds of financing, including the pre-seed stage, when founders develop an idea and work towards a minimum viable product (MVP); the seed stage, when they refine the MVP for market fit; and the series A to C stages, when they scale the business, before exiting through an initial public offering or an acquisition.

According to a recent Our Hong Kong Foundation report, only 10 per cent of founders in the city received support from venture capital or angel investors, 30 per cent got funding from the government, and 85 per cent had to tap personal savings.
But the report highlighted a stark imbalance in the government’s funding allocation.
As of 2024, funding was concentrated heavily at the pre-seed stage, at HK$49.5 billion, and in late-stage investment beyond series C, at HK$62 billion, leaving those in between – often described as the “valley of death” – largely underserved, with only HK$3.4 billion in capital support.
Apart from a lack of funding and support, Hong Kong founders have complained on online forums about high office rents, talent costs and the city’s small market size, with some pointing to places such as Bangkok and Shenzhen as better choices.
Headwinds
Alberto Moel, a professor of practice in finance at the University of Hong Kong, said it would be harder for young entrepreneurs such as Wong and Mochizuki to grow businesses built from their own ideas in the city, as the government and universities dominated the local start-up ecosystem.
“We are in a stage in Hong Kong where university research projects are the ones driving the pool of innovation,” he said.
“If your idea is outside that pool, then you are basically up against the usual headwinds in venture capital that have been around for a long time, namely that it is difficult to get capital and difficult to put together a team.”
Moel added that Hong Kong’s risk-averse culture was also reflected in the investment behaviour of venture capitalists, resulting in limited capital for very early stage start-ups or those taking on more risk.
In contrast, funding for such companies in the US was much broader because the culture there was more inclined to “try things and see what happens”, while there was much more capital in the country, he said.
Hong Kong’s young entrepreneurs would stand a better chance of success if they looked at opportunities arising from university research projects, Moel said.
“If the policy is not focused on [independent ideas], you are more likely to fail, and it is going to discourage you,” he said.
“I would recommend young entrepreneurs look at the existing platforms and work within them because you will find much better chances and opportunities to monetise [ideas] into a company.”
The government should do more to publicise and create opportunities for building businesses from research projects by linking tech-minded businesspeople with innovative ideas, he added.
Derek Chim, HKSTP’s head of start-up ecosystem and development, agreed that access to early-stage capital remained important in helping innovative ventures scale up, and said the park had teamed up with the private sector to catalyse start-up growth.
“While different investors naturally have different risk appetites and return expectations, we are seeing growing interest in deep-tech and innovation-driven companies that require longer development horizons,” he said.

The Innovation, Technology and Industry Bureau said the government attached importance to encouraging and cultivating a thriving I&T ecosystem for start-ups, and acknowledged that its sustainability relied heavily on private sector participation.
It said the government would launch an HK$10 billion Innovation and Technology Industry-Oriented Fund this year to channel more social capital into “emerging and future industries of strategic importance”, benefiting companies at different stages of development.
Despite the growing range of start-up funding options in Hong Kong, Mochizuki and Wong agreed the city’s cautious culture still made it hard for young entrepreneurs to strike out on their own.
“In Hong Kong, the culture drives most people down a very traditional path – primary school, high school, graduating from college, working in a full-time job – and it is very hard to pivot if you want to change your profession based on your interests,” Wong said.
“Everything is laid out for you, and this sense of security is embedded into young Hong Kong people growing up.”
